headline: Lab experiment shows how electrons gain energy during magnetic reconnection
author: Sam Jarman

paragraphs.text: November 28, 2026 report
by Sam Jarman, Phys.org
edited by Gaby Clark, reviewed by Robert Egan

Within a plasma, magnetic field lines can break apart and join up again in a new arrangement, releasing huge amounts of stored magnetic energy in the process. Named magnetic reconnection, this phenomenon is known to power dramatic solar flares and has also been recreated in lab experiments on Earth.
So far, however, some key details about the process remain poorly understood. In particular, physicists have yet to explain how energy is transferred to a plasma's electrons during reconnection.

Through new research published in Physical Review Letters, a team led by Sonu Yadav at West Virginia University has found direct evidence that this handover is carried out by "lower-hybrid drift waves": ripples that form at the sharp boundaries created by reconnection.
Elusive energy boost

To date, physicists have proposed several ways that electrons could be indirectly energized by reconnection. Previous theories have suggested that while some electrons may be sped up directly by the electric fields the process creates, others gain energy by bouncing off shrinking loops of magnetic field.

A combination of simulations, lab experiments and spacecraft observations has now all pointed to lower-hybrid drift waves as another possibility: these waves form where the plasma's density drops steeply over a short distance, which is exactly what happens at the edges of reconnection regions. Until now, however, researchers had yet to observe how electrons respond to these waves.
Merging plasma

To address the challenge, Yadav's team used the PHASMA facility at West Virginia University: a vacuum chamber almost 5 meters (16 feet) long. Inside, they created two twisted columns of magnetized helium plasma and pushed them together to trigger reconnection.

Because each merger played out in almost exactly the same way, the researchers could run the experiment many times. In some runs, they measured the waves with electrical probes—while in others, they recorded the electrons' speeds by measuring their scattering of laser light. They then compared their observations with theoretical predictions for lower-hybrid drift waves.
Electron energy transfer

As the waves grew, extra clusters of electrons appeared at speeds matching how fast the waves moved along the magnetic field. Over around two microseconds, these peaks spread out into flat regions in the electrons' range of speeds, closely matching the team's theoretical predictions.

The same electron signatures also appeared at two different points along the reconnection boundary, showing that the effect wasn't limited to a single spot. Together, the results suggest that the waves act as go-betweens, passing magnetic energy to the electrons.

Yadav's team now hopes their result could help to solve a key mystery of magnetic reconnection by giving theories of wave-driven electron heating a benchmark to test against. It could also help researchers to improve their models of energy flow within plasma, and perhaps even make better sense of spacecraft measurements close to sites where magnetic reconnection occurs.
